lesson.title: Checking the Seams: Continuity of Piecewise Functions
lesson.summary: A piecewise function can only be continuous if each individual piece is continuous on its own interval and the pieces also agree in value and in one-sided limit at every point where the definition switches.
lesson.body:
A piecewise function is built by gluing together separate formulas, each one valid on its own sub-interval of the domain. Checking whether such a function is continuous takes two distinct kinds of work. Inside each piece, away from any boundary, continuity is usually easy to confirm, since most individual pieces are polynomials, roots, or other familiar continuous functions, and continuity there follows the same rules as continuity on an interval covered earlier. The real work happens exactly at the breakpoints, the x values where the definition switches from one formula to another, since that is the only place a piecewise function is at any real risk of having a discontinuity.

At a breakpoint x = b, checking continuity means directly applying the one-sided continuity ideas from earlier. Compute f(b) using whichever formula the piecewise definition assigns to that point. Compute the left-hand limit using the formula that governs x values just below b, and the right-hand limit using the formula that governs x values just above b. The function is continuous at b exactly when all three numbers agree: the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and f(b) itself. If any two of those three disagree, the function has a discontinuity at that seam, and the earlier classification, removable, jump, or infinite, describes exactly what kind.

Worked example: let f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x <= 1, and f(x) = 3x - 1 for x > 1. Away from x = 1, both pieces are polynomials, so both are automatically continuous on their own open intervals. At the breakpoint x = 1, compute f(1) using the first formula, since x = 1 satisfies x <= 1: f(1) = 1^2 + 1 = 2. Compute the left-hand limit using the same formula: lim(x to 1-) (x^2 + 1) = 1 + 1 = 2. Compute the right-hand limit using the second formula: lim(x to 1+) (3x - 1) = 3(1) - 1 = 2. All three values equal 2, so f is continuous at x = 1, and therefore continuous on the entire real line, since every other point was already covered by one of the two polynomial pieces.

A second example shows how a seam can fail. Let g(x) = x + 2 for x < 0, and g(x) = x^2 for x >= 0. At the breakpoint, g(0) = 0^2 = 0, using the second formula since x = 0 satisfies x >= 0. The left-hand limit is lim(x to 0-) (x + 2) = 0 + 2 = 2. The right-hand limit is lim(x to 0+) x^2 = 0. Here g(0) = 0 matches the right-hand limit, so g is right-continuous at 0, but the left-hand limit of 2 does not match, so g is not left-continuous, and therefore not continuous at x = 0 overall. Because both one-sided limits, 2 and 0, exist as finite numbers but disagree, this is a jump discontinuity of size 2, sitting right at the seam between the two pieces.

The general lesson is that a piecewise function is only as continuous as its worst seam. Every individual piece can be perfectly smooth, built from familiar continuous functions, and the overall function can still fail to be continuous if the pieces do not meet up correctly where they change over. This is why checking piecewise continuity always comes down to the same short checklist at each breakpoint: confirm the function value, confirm both one-sided limits, and confirm all three agree, exactly the machinery introduced for continuity at a point and one-sided continuity.
